newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian banks shift to credits from securities mkt.
newsitem.headline: Russian banks shift to credits from securities mkt.

text.p: Russian banks, facing falling yields on government securities, are shifting to their main business of granting credits to industry, a senior central bank official said on Thursday.

"Under the influence of falling GKO (Treasury bill) yields and shrinking possibilities to speculate on the foreign exchange market, banks have to start specialising in offering loans," central bank Prudential Supervision Department Head Mikhail Sukhov told a banking congress.
Sukhov said the total number of banks operating on the credit market had risen to 38 percent of the total number of banks from 35 percent in the first quarter.

Yelena Chekmaryova, head of the bank's Research, Information and Statistics Department, said the average interest rate on bank credits had fallen to 45 percent from 61 percent at the start of the year.

T-bill yields have fallen to about 22 percent from 200 percent last summer and the central bank says the yield will slip to 20 percent by the end of the year. Ministers expect inflation of around 12 percent this year.
The possibility of speculation on the foreign exchange market plummeted after the central bank introduced its sloping corridor programme two years ago.
Under the policy, the central bank sets a band within which the rouble can fluctuate against the dollar and announces daily buy/sell rates. The rouble has never strayed from the corridor.

But Sukhov said few Russian banks could offer loans as most of them have an authorised capital of less than 10 billion roubles. Only less than 20 percent have an authorised capital of over 30 billion roubles.
He said less than 200 banks out of Russia's 2,000 accounted for the growth in credit granting.
Many banks fear granting credits to Russia's ailing industry, but syndicated loans are still rare, Sukhov said.
Firms for their part say high real interest rates, along with a heavy and arbitrary tax burden, are strangling production and stifling the economy.
Sukhov also said the number of banks involved in operations on the stock market rose to five percent from three percent in the middle of 1996.
